rv.q: Set in a dreary constituency office close to the Nottinghamshire village where Graham grew up, it charts the career of fictitious politico David Lyons.
It gets to the heart of the ideological rifts and tiffs that have beset Labour since its divisive fightback against the humiliations of the Thatcher years.

This is a very clever play by the political anorak and wunderkind James Graham, who seems to be prolific to the point of tireless, with another play, Ink, already in the West End. Clearly this one was a labour of love for him too. Here he’s on a mission to show us how the Labour Party loves to self- destruct.

‘This House’, his thriller about the minority Labour government of the 1970s, is one of the great plays of our time, while ‘Ink’, his sinuous drama about Rupert Murdoch’s sulphurous rise, is currently packing ‘em in at the Duke ofYork’s Theatre.

Georgie, an American woman in her 40s who works as a receptionist at a London school, kissesAlex, a butcher in his 70s, claiming to have mistaken him for someone else. This turns out to be a fabrication. Georgie is somewhat loose with the truth.

The BIG sensation in London Theatre at the moment is the young playwright James Graham. In a few short years he’s gone from pub theatre to having two major plays running in the West End, in neighbouring theatres on St Martins Lane. He really is an extraordinary talent and his work is incomparable with anyone else.
